title: Passwordless Authentication
summary: Passwordless authentication is a set of authentication methods in which the user proves possession of a registered authenticator bound to their identity and never supplies a shared secret that can be phished, reused or cracked offline. The two dominant families are asymmetric key credentials based on the Web Authentication standard, where the private key stays in a hardware security key or platform authenticator and the public key is registered with the relying party, and certificate-based authentication, where a device or smart card certificate issued by enterprise certificate authority replaces the password. Both defeat password-centric attacks structurally rather than by policy: there is no secret to spray, no hash to crack, no code to relay to a waitress-style adversary-in-the-middle proxy, and the signature is bound to the origin so that a lookalike domain cannot harvest a usable response. Passkeys extend the same primitive to consumer use by synchronising or device-linking credentials, which improves usability and recovery but changes the threat model, since the credential now follows the user's platform account rather than a single physical token. Deployment work is mostly in the unglamorous details: recovery and enrolment, because account recovery becomes the weakest authentication path once passwords are gone; attestation and device inventory, to decide which authenticators are acceptable; account identifier design, to avoid silently re-enrolling a credential to the wrong person; and legacy systems that cannot speak the protocol and therefore need a brokered or certificate-based compromise. Hybrid environments usually run passwordless for interactive users and retain vaulted secrets for machine identities, where the equivalent control is short-lived certificates and automatic rotation.
objectives: You will be able to explain how asymmetric key credentials resist phishing and credential replay structurally rather than by policy.
You will be able to compare hardware security keys, platform authenticators and synchronised passkeys by assurance and usability.
You will be able to design enrolment and recovery procedures that do not reintroduce a weak authentication path.
You will be able to identify systems that cannot support passwordless authentication and select a brokered or certificate-based alternative.
You will be able to detect suspicious authenticator registration, deletion and re-registration events in identity provider logs.
You will be able to plan a phased migration that keeps break-glass access available without standing passwords for administrators.

beginner.definition: Passwordless authentication lets you sign in without typing a shared secret. Instead, you use something tied to you, such as a security key, your fingerprint, or your phone. The secret never leaves your device. Attackers cannot steal what you never send.
beginner.whyItMatters: Passwords are guessable, reusable, and easy to trick out of people. Even a second code can be relayed by a fake login page. Passwordless sign-in removes the shared secret completely, so a fake page has nothing useful to copy. The remaining risk moves to account recovery, which needs just as much care.
howItWorks: You register a device or a security key with your account, once.
The device creates a key pair, which is a matched set of two keys.
The public key goes to the service, and the private key stays on your device.
To sign in, the service sends a random challenge, which is a fresh question.
Your device signs that challenge, and the service checks the signature.
beginner.example: Think of a wax seal on a letter. Anyone can look at the seal, but only you own the stamp. A forger cannot copy the stamp from the wax mark alone. Each letter gets a different seal, so an old one is useless. That is why a copied sign-in page cannot replay your answer.
takeaways: Passwordless sign-in uses a key on your device, not a shared secret.
No shared secret means nothing useful for a fake login page to copy.
Protect account recovery, because it becomes the easiest way in.
